items.stem: A gambler starts with Rs. 10 against an adversary with unlimited capital. On each play he wins Rs. 1 with probability 2/3 and loses Rs. 1 otherwise. The probability of the gambler's ultimate ruin is
items.explanation: The game favours the gambler (p = 2/3 > q = 1/3), so ruin is not certain. Against an opponent with unlimited money, P(ruin starting from Rs. a) = (q/p)^a. Here q/p = 1/3/2/3 = 1/2 and a = 10, so the ruin probability is (1/2)^10. Trap: (q)^a or 1 − p^a ignores that the walk can move up and come back down many times.

items.stem: Customers arrive at a counter as a Poisson process with rate 3 per minute. Given that the time between two successive arrivals is more than 1 minutes, the probability that it is more than 3 minutes is
items.explanation: Gaps between Poisson arrivals are exponential with rate λ = 3, and the exponential distribution is memoryless: having waited 1 minutes, the extra wait is again exponential. So P(T > 3 | T > 1) = P(T > 2) = e^(−λ·2) = e^(−6). Trap: e^(−λ·3) uses the full 3 minutes and ignores the condition.

items.stem: Let N₁(t) and N₂(t) be independent Poisson processes with rates λ and 2λ respectively. Then P(N₁(t) = 1 | N₁(t) + N₂(t) = 4) is
items.explanation: Given that 4 events occurred in total, each one came from the first process independently with probability λ/(λ + 2λ) = 1/3. So N₁(t) given the total is Binomial(4, 1/3): P = C(4,1)(1/3)^1(2/3)^3 = 32/81. The time t and λ cancel out. Trap: swapping the two probabilities gives 8/81; dropping the binomial coefficient gives 8/81.

items.stem: A three-state Markov chain has transition matrix P = [[q, p, 0], [q, 0, p], [0, q, p]] with p = 1/3 and q = 1 − p. The 3-step transition probability p₁₂⁽³⁾ is
items.explanation: An n-step transition probability is an entry of Pⁿ: p₁₂⁽³⁾ is row 1, column 2 of P^3. Row 1 of P^2 is (2/3, 2/9, 1/9); multiplying it by column 2 of P gives 8/27. Trap: (p₁₂)^3 multiplies one-step probabilities along a single path and misses the other paths.

items.stem: A three-state Markov chain has transition matrix P = [[q, p, 0], [q, 0, p], [0, q, p]] with p = 1/3 and q = 1 − p. The first-passage probability f₁₂⁽⁴⁾ (first visit to state 2 at step 4, starting from state 1) is
items.explanation: A first passage at step 4 means the chain is NOT in state 2 at steps 1 to 3 and IS there at step 4. Track the probability of every state step by step, setting state 2 to zero after each step before step 4 (a 'taboo' calculation). This gives f₁₂⁽⁴⁾ = 8/81. Trap: the ordinary 4-step probability p₁₂⁽⁴⁾ = 22/81 also counts paths that reached state 2 earlier.
